title: Thallium Toxicity -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Thallium is a tasteless, odorless, water-soluble element associated with both accidental intoxication and intentional poisoning. The occupational exposure limit is 0.1 mg/m³ for up to 8 hours per day, while concentrations at or above 15 mg/m³ are considered acutely hazardous. Absorption occurs readily through inhalational and dermal routes.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Thallium toxicity presents a substantial public health concern, particularly in settings involving industrial use or environmental contamination. Workers in electronics production, glass manufacturing, and related industries face the highest occupational risk. Additional exposure pathways include ingestion or inhalation of contaminated food, water, or soil. Populations residing near hazardous waste sites and individuals exposed to illicit pesticide or rodenticide formulations also represent vulnerable groups.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Evaluation requires careful clinical assessment supported by targeted diagnostic testing. Manifestations are often nonspecific, including gastrointestinal disturbance and progressive neurologic dysfunction, which may deter early recognition. Confirmation relies on elevated serum thallium concentrations and increased 24-hour urinary excretion. Management emphasizes prompt elimination through decontamination, Prussian blue therapy, and hemodialysis in severe cases. Supportive measures are essential for mitigating systemic effects and preventing long-term complications.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Introduction
content: Thallium (Tl; atomic number 81) is a heavy metal associated with a broad spectrum of toxic effects in humans. [1] Thallium sulfate was historically employed as an ant and rat poison. [2] [3] [4] The occupational exposure limit for thallium on the skin is 0.1 mg/m³ over 8 hours, with concentrations of 15 mg/m³ or higher considered immediately hazardous to health. (Source: Occupational Safety and Health Administration , 2021) Thallium is readily absorbed via dermal and inhalational routes. This element's tasteless, odorless, and water-soluble properties have contributed to reports of both accidental and intentional poisoning.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Introduction
content: Historically, thallium salts were used therapeutically to treat dermatophytosis. The radioactive isotope thallium-201, typically administered as thallous chloride, was widely used for cardiac stress tests before being replaced by technetium-99m as the preferred tracer in nuclear medicine. Thallium-201 remains in use for the evaluation of coronary artery disease. The radioactive form exhibits toxicity more than 4,000 times lower than the elemental metal. Thallium scintigraphy assesses tissue perfusion by measuring thallium uptake. Normal coronary arteries dilate in response to exercise or vasodilatory drugs, potentially reducing myocardial perfusion in adjacent regions, a phenomenon termed "coronary steal syndrome." [5]

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Introduction
content: Thallium is a gray posttransition metal that does not occur in its free form in nature. Although chemically similar to tin, isolated thallium undergoes discoloration upon exposure to air. Exposure occurs primarily through dermal absorption, inhalation, or ingestion. [6]

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Etiology
content: Thallium was banned from household use in the US. in 1965 and commercial use in 1975. Thallium intoxication frequently mimics other medical conditions, resulting in underrecognition and delayed diagnosis. More recently, thallium has found applications in the semiconductor and optical industries. Historical use as an insecticide and rodenticide, combined with its tasteless and odorless properties, has contributed to accidental poisonings and, in some cases, intentional administration.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Etiology
content: Although thallium is no longer employed as a pesticide in the US., its use persists in some countries. Contamination of Chinese herbal medications with this element has been reported. Toxic exposure can occur cumulatively via dermal, inhalational, or gastrointestinal routes. Accidental insufflation or injection in individuals using cocaine or intravenous opioids, as well as dermal absorption through protective gloves, has also been documented. [7] [8] [9] Causes of thallium toxicity include occupational exposure, ingestion of contaminated substances, contaminated drug use, consumption of contaminated foods such as fish, exposure to hazardous waste sites, and intentional poisoning. [10]

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Epidemiology
content: Within the US, 60 single exposures to thallium were reported to the National Poison Data Center in 2023, with only 1 major outcome and no fatalities. [11] Internationally, thallium toxicity is more common in developing countries, although epidemiologic data are limited. Mortality from acute thallium poisoning is estimated at 6% to 15%, with a lethal dose ranging from 10 to 15 mg/kg. Fatalities may occur at lower exposures. Demographic information, including age, sex, and race, is currently unavailable.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Pathophysiology
content: Thallium is chemically analogous to potassium and is treated as such at the cellular level. Five major toxicologic mechanisms characterize thallium toxicity.
contents: Thallium Toxicity -- Pathophysiology. Thallium is chemically analogous to potassium and is treated as such at the cellular level. Five major toxicologic mechanisms characterize thallium toxicity.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Pathophysiology
content: First, this posttransition metal can accumulate in tissues with high potassium concentrations, initially stimulating and subsequently inhibiting potassium-dependent processes. Inhibition of pyruvate kinase and succinate dehydrogenase disrupts the Krebs cycle and glucose metabolism, reducing adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production and impairing sodium-potassium ATPase activity, which leads to cellular swelling and vacuolization. Second, thallium sequesters riboflavin and inhibits flavin adenine dinucleotide, disrupting the electron transport chain and further decreasing ATP synthesis.

Inhibition of pyruvate kinase and succinate dehydrogenase disrupts the Krebs cycle and glucose metabolism, reducing adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production and impairing sodium-potassium ATPase activity, which leads to cellular swelling and vacuolization. Second, thallium sequesters riboflavin and inhibits flavin adenine dinucleotide, disrupting the electron transport chain and further decreasing ATP synthesis.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Pathophysiology
content: Third, thallium exhibits high affinity for sulfur in disulfide bonds, disrupting cysteine cross-linking and impairing keratin formation. Fourth, this toxic heavy metal interferes with protein synthesis, particularly affecting the 60S ribosomal subunit. Fifth, thallium induces myelin degeneration in both the central and peripheral nervous systems, although the precise mechanism remains unknown.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Toxicokinetics
content: Thallium exhibits 3 toxicokinetic phases. During the intravascular distribution phase, occurring within the first 4 hours postexposure, the metal is transported to various organs via the bloodstream. The central nervous system distribution phase follows, spanning approximately 4 to 48 hours, during which thallium penetrates neural tissue. The elimination phase begins around 24 hours postexposure and proceeds primarily through renal excretion and fecal elimination. This phase is prolonged, with complete clearance potentially requiring up to 30 days.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- History and Physical -- Acute versus Chronic Exposure
content: Initial symptoms of thallium toxicity involve gastrointestinal, neurological, and dermatological systems. Delayed alopecia is a hallmark of acute poisoning. Acute manifestations persist in cases of prolonged exposure, with neurological effects continuing despite decreasing blood thallium concentrations.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- History and Physical -- Manifestations of Thallium Toxicity
content: Gastrointestinal symptoms appear within 3 to 4 hours of exposure and include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea or constipation, and, rarely, hematemesis or melena. Neurologic symptoms typically develop 2 to 5 days postexposure and comprise ascending, often severely painful peripheral neuropathies, distal motor weakness, ataxia, tremor, and cranial nerve deficits.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- History and Physical -- Manifestations of Thallium Toxicity
content: Dermatologic findings initially include nonspecific features, such as scaling and acneiform or pustular eruptions. Alopecia develops after 2 to 3 weeks due to the disruption of cysteine disulfide bonds. Mees lines appear on the nails approximately 1 month postexposure. Additional dermatologic manifestations include hypohidrosis or anhidrosis and painful glossitis.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- History and Physical -- Manifestations of Thallium Toxicity
content: Ocular manifestations encompass diplopia, ptosis, 7th cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuropathy, and lens opacities. Cardiovascular effects may include tachycardia and hypertension. Additional systemic manifestations include headache, seizures, insomnia, and, in severe cases, coma. Fatal outcomes may occur.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: Examination should prioritize affected regions while maintaining a comprehensive assessment, including neurologic, ophthalmologic, and gastrointestinal evaluations. Gastrointestinal assessment should include abdominal examination, rectal examination, and stool guaiac testing. Neurologic evaluation should assess all cranial nerves and examine for nystagmus and ptosis. Assessment of lower extremities should include strength testing and evaluation of sensation to pinprick, touch, temperature, vibration, and proprioception. Severely painful peripheral neuropathy represents a classic manifestation of thallium poisoning. Ophthalmologic evaluation should include slit-lamp and funduscopic examinations, as well as assessment of visual acuity and color vision.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Evaluation
content: Elevated thallium concentrations in hair, nails, blood, urine, feces, and saliva can assist in establishing a diagnosis, with 24-hour urine collection analyzed by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) considered the standard method. Although hair, saliva, and feces testing have been utilized, urine analysis is preferred for clinical purposes. Atomic absorption spectroscopy may be employed but is less accurate than ICP-MS. Spot urine testing offers faster results but carries a high false-positive rate, and blood thallium concentrations may yield false-negative results. Additional laboratory evaluation should include complete blood count with differential, electrolytes, glucose, blood urea nitrogen, liver function tests, and calcium. Thallium is radiopaque. Radiographs may detect the presence of the metal following ingestion.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Evaluation
content: Ancillary testing is indicated for specific complications. Electrocardiography should be performed to evaluate arrhythmias. Electroencephalography is recommended for seizure-like activity. Nerve conduction studies are indicated in patients with neurologic symptoms.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Treatment / Management
content: Much like other toxic exposures, initial management begins with stabilization of the airway, breathing, and circulation, along with removal of contaminated clothing. Activated charcoal, Prussian blue, or both may be used for internal decontamination following ingestion and should be administered as early as possible. [12] [13]

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Treatment / Management
content: For dermal exposure, affected skin should be washed thoroughly with soap and water. In cases of ocular exposure, the eyes should be irrigated with room-temperature water or saline. Activated charcoal and Prussian blue may be administered for gastrointestinal ingestion.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Treatment / Management
content: Prussian blue is the treatment of choice for thallium poisoning, reducing enterohepatic recirculation and enhancing elimination. The typical dose is 250 mg/kg per day, divided into 2 or 4 doses. A definitive endpoint of therapy has not been established. Prussian blue may be suspended in 15% mannitol or administered with polyethylene glycol in patients with constipation.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Treatment / Management
content: Compared to activated charcoal, Prussian blue is more effective and is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. [14] Multidose activated charcoal should be employed when Prussian blue is unavailable.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Treatment / Management
content: Hemodialysis may also facilitate thallium elimination. The use of this intervention is generally limited to cases in which gastrointestinal decontamination with Prussian blue or activated charcoal is not feasible. Consultation with a medical toxicologist and nephrologist is recommended when considering extracorporeal elimination procedures, such as hemodialysis.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Thallium toxicity presents like other toxic syndromes and various medical conditions. The following alternative diagnoses should be considered alongside this entity: Toxic syndromes Carbon monoxide Arsenic Isoniazid Mercury Organophosphates Botulism Other medical conditions Thiamine deficiency Diabetic polyneuritis Acute and chronic demyelinating disease Vasculitis Poliomyelitis

content: Thallium poisoning can be challenging to diagnose due to its resemblance to the above conditions. title: Thallium Toxicity -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis for patients with thallium toxicity depends on the ingested dose and the presence of neurological symptoms. Patients with minimal manifestations may recover fully with treatment, whereas individuals with severe toxicity can experience persistent alopecia, neuropathy, and psychiatric effects.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Prognosis
content: Early diagnosis and treatment are associated with a better prognosis. [15] Neurologic damage may persist if gastrointestinal decontamination is delayed. Signs and symptoms of peripheral neuropathy can continue for many years after poisoning, most commonly involving painful neuropathy of the lower extremities.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Complications
content: Neurological damage may be persistent, with involvement of the lower extremities most commonly reported. Alopecia is frequent. Documented psychiatric manifestations include agitation, aggression, depression, psychosis, and personality changes. [16]

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Consultations
content: Consultation with a medical toxicologist or a poison center is recommended for any patient with suspected thallium poisoning. This consultation can provide expert guidance on diagnosis, management, decontamination, complication monitoring, laboratory interpretation, and interprofessional coordination to optimize outcomes for patients with this condition.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patients unintentionally exposed to thallium should wash affected skin with tap water and remove contaminated clothing promptly. Intentional ingestions require psychiatric evaluation once the patient is stable. Oral hygiene should be closely monitored. Shaving the patient’s head may reduce stress from hair loss and improve morale. All patients should receive close follow-up care.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Thallium toxicity should be managed by an interprofessional team, including an emergency medicine physician, medical toxicologist, internist, neurologist, nurse practitioner, and intensivist. The triage nurse should follow protocols for patients suspected of poisoning, including potential decontamination. The emergency care provider should communicate with the interprofessional team.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Initial management of thallium toxicity requires assessment of the airway, breathing, circulation, and the need for decontamination. Nurses play an active role in resuscitation by establishing intravenous access, providing oxygenation, documenting the event, and placing the patient on monitoring devices. Activated charcoal may be administered to patients presenting within an hour of ingestion. Dermal exposure necessitates washing the skin with soap and water. Ocular exposure requires copious irrigation with room-temperature water or saline.

title: Thallium Toxicity -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Activated charcoal and Prussian blue may be used for gastrointestinal ingestion. Prussian blue has demonstrated greater efficacy and is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Once resuscitation is complete, the events leading to thallium ingestion should be carefully reviewed. If ingestion was intentional, a mental health nurse should evaluate the patient prior to discharge. Finally, evaluation by a neurologist is recommended to determine the extent of neurological deficits. Open communication among interprofessional team members can help limit morbidity associated with thallium toxicity.
